records.name: Steelman first

origin.author: Daniel Dennett (Rapoport's rules)
origin.work: Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking

records.summary: Before criticising, restate the position so well its holder would wish they had said it that way, note points of agreement and what you learned. Only then attack.
records.key_question: Could the author of this idea have stated it better than I just did?
use_when: I think their argument is wrong
make the strongest case for it
am I being fair to this idea
records.produces: the strongest version of the position, points of agreement and what you learned, written before any critique
records.failure_mode: Restating a weaker version and attacking that.

records.name: Red team

origin.author: Military and intelligence practice; Micah Zenko

records.summary: An independent group adopts the adversary's goals and tries to make the plan fail. Independence and licence to win are what make it work.
records.key_question: If I wanted this to fail, where would I attack?
use_when: how would a competitor beat this
records.produces: a list of attacks from the adversary's point of view, ranked by damage and likelihood
records.failure_mode: A red team without independence or permission to win, which produces polite feedback.
steps: Write the plan and its goal in a few sentences.
Define the adversary: who wants this to fail, and what they can do.
Adopt the adversary's goals fully; do not defend the plan.
List every way to make the plan fail.
Rank attacks by damage and likelihood.
Hand the top attacks back to the plan's owner for answers.

records.name: Dialectical inquiry

origin.author: Richard Mason; David Schweiger et al.
origin.work: A Dialectical Approach to Strategic Planning; Group approaches for improving strategic decision making

records.summary: Build a full counter-plan resting on opposite assumptions and debate the two. Stronger than lone devil's advocacy because it forces a whole alternative to exist.
records.key_question: What plan rests on the opposite assumptions, and how well does it hold up?
records.evidence_note: Dialectical inquiry and devil's advocacy both beat consensus approaches on decision quality (Schweiger, Sandberg & Ragan 1986).
use_when: test our core assumptions against an alternative
records.produces: a full counter-plan built on the opposite assumptions, and the assumptions that survived the debate
records.failure_mode: A counter-plan built as a straw man so the original wins easily.
steps: List the assumptions the current plan rests on.
Negate each key assumption.
Build a complete, plausible counter-plan from the negated assumptions.
Debate the two plans assumption by assumption.
Keep the assumptions that survive and rebuild the plan on them.

records.name: Devil's advocate
records.summary: One role argues against the proposal. Effective only if the role is genuine and protected; a token advocate makes the group more confident, not less.
records.key_question: Is anyone actually arguing the other side, with licence to win?
records.produces: the strongest arguments against the proposal, each with what it would take to answer it
records.failure_mode: A token advocate whose objections are dismissed, which raises the group's confidence.
steps: Assign the role openly and protect it from social cost.
State the proposal as it stands.
Argue against it as strongly as possible, without hedging.
List each objection with the evidence that would answer it.
Have the group answer each objection before deciding.

records.name: Consider the opposite

origin.author: Charles Lord, Mark Lepper, Elizabeth Preston

records.summary: Ask how you would evaluate the evidence if it had pointed the other way. More effective than simply being told to be unbiased.
records.key_question: Would I accept this evidence if it supported the opposite conclusion?
records.evidence_note: Consider-the-opposite reduced biased assimilation where instructions to be fair did not (Lord, Lepper & Preston 1984). Replicated in debiasing literature.
use_when: the evidence supports what I already think
what if the data pointed the other way
records.produces: the evidence re-read as if it had come out the other way, with the interpretation that changed
records.failure_mode: Imagining the opposite result only briefly and returning to the same reading.

records.name: Analysis of competing hypotheses
records.summary: List every hypothesis, list the evidence, mark each piece as consistent or inconsistent with each hypothesis. Keep the hypothesis with the least evidence against it, not the most for it.
records.key_question: Which hypothesis has the least evidence against it?
use_when: which explanation fits the evidence best
records.produces: a matrix of hypotheses against evidence with the least-contradicted hypothesis identified
records.failure_mode: Counting supporting evidence instead of looking for inconsistencies.
steps: List every plausible hypothesis, including ones you dislike.
List the significant evidence and arguments.
Mark each item as consistent, inconsistent or neutral with each hypothesis.
Drop evidence that fits all hypotheses equally; it does not discriminate.
Rank hypotheses by how much evidence is inconsistent with each.
Name what new evidence would most change the ranking.

records.name: Key assumptions check
records.summary: List every assumption the conclusion rests on, rate how well supported each is, and name what would make it false. Shows which unexamined assumption carries the most weight.
records.key_question: Which assumption, if false, brings the whole conclusion down?
use_when: check the assumptions in this plan
what has to be true for this to work
records.produces: a list of assumptions rated by support, with what would make each false and the weakest load-bearing one marked
records.failure_mode: Listing only assumptions that are easy to defend.
steps: Write the conclusion or plan.
List every assumption it depends on, stated and unstated.
Rate each: well supported, partly supported, unsupported.
For each, write what would make it false.
Mark the assumptions that carry the most weight and are least supported.

records.name: Find the crux
records.summary: Find the single belief which, if it changed, would change your conclusion. Disagreement worth having is about that belief.
records.key_question: What single belief, if I changed it, would change my conclusion?
records.produces: the single belief that would flip the conclusion, and what evidence would settle it
records.failure_mode: Naming a belief that would not actually change the conclusion if it flipped.
steps: State your conclusion and the other side's.
List the beliefs each conclusion depends on.
For each belief, ask: if this changed, would my conclusion change?
Keep the one belief that would flip it.
Name the evidence or test that would settle that belief.

records.name: Chesterton's fence
records.summary: Do not remove a rule or structure until you know why it was put there. The reason may still apply.
records.key_question: Do I know why this was built before I propose removing it?
use_when: let's just get rid of this rule
why do we do it this way
records.produces: the original reason for the rule or structure, and whether it still applies
records.failure_mode: Assuming no reason exists because none is written down.

records.name: Extraordinary claims
records.summary: The evidence required scales with how much the claim contradicts what is already well established.
records.key_question: How surprising is this claim, and is the evidence proportionate?
use_when: this sounds too good to be true
records.produces: the claim rated against established knowledge, with the strength of evidence it would need
records.failure_mode: Demanding extraordinary evidence for claims that are merely unfamiliar to you.

records.name: Lateral reading

origin.author: Sam Wineburg & Sarah McGrew
origin.work: Lateral Reading (Stanford History Education Group working paper)

records.summary: Judge a source by leaving it: check what other independent sources say about who is behind it, before reading it closely.
records.key_question: What do independent sources say about who produced this?
records.evidence_note: Professional fact-checkers outperformed historians and students by reading laterally (Wineburg & McGrew 2017). Training studies show gains.
records.produces: a note on who is behind the source and what independent sources say about it
records.failure_mode: Reading the source closely before checking who it is, which lets its presentation persuade you.
steps: Before reading closely, leave the page.
Search for the organisation or author behind it.
Read what independent, reputable sources say about them.
Check funding, affiliations and track record.
Return to the source only if it passes.

records.name: Pre-commit update triggers
records.summary: Before seeing new evidence, state what result would move your estimate and by how much. Prevents re-reading any evidence as confirmation.
records.key_question: What result would make me change my mind, decided before I see it?
use_when: set criteria before seeing the results
I keep reading everything as confirmation
how should this new data change my view
records.produces: a pre-registered list of results and the size of the update each would cause
records.failure_mode: Writing triggers so vague that any result can be read as meeting or missing them.

records.name: Survival score

origin.author: Panta Rhei (original)
origin.note: Original to Panta Rhei; describe as such.

records.summary: After the attacks, rate how much of the idea survives on a 0–10 scale, with the rule: one fatal flaw caps the score at 3, regardless of how many strengths there are.
records.key_question: After the strongest attack, how much of this is still standing?
use_when: how much of this idea survives
score this plan after the critique
is this idea still worth pursuing
records.produces: a 0 to 10 survival score with the fatal flaw, if any, and the strongest surviving element
records.failure_mode: Averaging strengths and weaknesses so a fatal flaw is diluted.
steps: List the attacks that landed and those that did not.
Check whether any attack is fatal on its own.
If one is, cap the score at 3.
Otherwise rate from 0 to 10 how much of the idea survives.
Write the strongest surviving element and the weakest link.

records.name: Subtraction

origin.author: Gabrielle Adams, Benjamin Converse, Andrew Hales, Leidy Klotz

records.summary: People default to adding when they improve something. Explicitly ask what to remove. The subtractive option is often cheaper and better, and is missed unless prompted.
records.key_question: What could I take away instead of adding?
records.evidence_note: Eight experiments, Nature 2021: participants overlooked subtractive solutions unless cued. Robust within the paradigm; applied effect sizes unknown.
records.card: Solve it only by removing things.
use_when: this process has too many steps
records.produces: a list of removable parts with the effect of removing each
records.failure_mode: Removing something that carried a real function that nobody wrote down.

records.name: Kill criteria
records.summary: Before committing, write the conditions and the date at which you will stop. Decided in advance, quitting does not depend on willpower in the moment.
records.key_question: What would have to happen, by when, for me to stop?
use_when: how will I know to stop
I keep throwing good money after bad
records.produces: written conditions and a date at which the commitment will be stopped
records.failure_mode: Kill criteria so loose they will never trigger.
steps: Write what you are committing to.
Write the signals that would show it is not working.
Turn each signal into a measurable condition.
Set a date to check.
Tell someone who will hold you to it.

records.name: Pre-mortem
records.summary: Imagine it is a year later and the decision failed. Write why. Imagined certainty of failure frees people to name risks they would otherwise keep quiet.
records.key_question: If this has failed a year from now, what is the most likely reason?
records.evidence_note: Prospective hindsight increased the number of reasons generated by about 30% (Mitchell, Russo & Pennington 1989). Effect on decision outcomes less studied.
use_when: what could go wrong with this
records.produces: a list of reasons the decision failed, ranked, with a mitigation for the top ones
records.failure_mode: Writing generic risks instead of specific stories of failure.
steps: Assume it is a year later and the decision has failed badly.
Everyone writes the reasons it failed, independently.
Pool the reasons and remove duplicates.
Rank by likelihood and impact.
Add mitigations or kill criteria for the top reasons.

records.name: Weighted criteria
records.summary: Name the criteria, weight them before scoring, score each option, sum. The value is in the weighting conversation; the total is only as good as the weights.
records.key_question: Did I set the weights before I saw the scores?
records.produces: a scoring table with weights set before scoring, totals, and a sensitivity check on the weights
records.failure_mode: Adjusting weights after scoring until the preferred option wins.
steps: List the options.
Name the criteria that matter.
Assign weights before looking at scores.
Score each option on each criterion.
Multiply and sum.
Check whether a reasonable change in weights changes the winner.

records.name: Differential diagnosis
records.summary: List every condition that could produce the symptoms, then order tests that discriminate between them, starting with the dangerous and the common.
records.key_question: Which test would tell my top two candidates apart?
use_when: what could be causing these symptoms
which test would tell them apart
records.produces: a ranked list of candidate causes with the test that discriminates between the top ones
records.failure_mode: Ordering tests by convenience and leaving the dangerous candidate untested.
steps: List every cause that could produce the observed symptoms.
Rank by likelihood and by danger if missed.
For the top candidates, find tests that would come out differently for each.
Run the most discriminating test first, starting with dangerous and common causes.
Update the list after each result.
